813.title: Thank your body
813.hook: this body carried you all the way here
813.howItsDone: Observant Jews say the Asher Yatzar blessing after using the bathroom, thanking God for the body's workings; some people of other paths practice a slow body scan with thanks, part by part.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ruth on the road and Paul greeting his friends by name. Your line was you mattered to me. Did your one plain sentence reach someone? Today, a thank-you to someone closer than any friend. Day eight hundred thirteen.

A heart keeps time through arguments, weddings and bad nights, without once asking to be noticed. Hands learn to hold a spoon, then a pen, then someone else's hand. A person can spend years criticizing a body and never once thank it. This block of the path has been about endings, and the body is the part of us that will one day end. Today: a psalm, a bathroom blessing and a letter of Paul's, each thanking it while it's still here.
screen: `A HEART, A PAIR OF HANDS.` → `NEVER ONCE THANKED.` → `THANKS WHILE IT'S HERE.`

segments.voice: First, fearfully and wonderfully made. In Psalm one hundred thirty-nine, the psalmist speaks to God about being formed before birth, and then says: "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works." Notice it isn't praise for a perfect body. It's praise for a made one, a body someone took care over. Second, a blessing for openings. Jewish tradition has a blessing called Asher Yatzar, said after using the bathroom. In paraphrase, it blesses God who formed the human body with wisdom, with openings and hollows, and it notes that if one of them were blocked or opened when it shouldn't be, a person couldn't stand and live. It's a thank-you for plumbing, said again and again through the day, and it's honest: it knows how fragile the whole thing is. Third, no part can say no need. In his first letter to the Corinthians, Paul uses the body as a picture of a community: "the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee: nor again the head to the feet, I have no need of you." He's talking about people in a church, but the picture works because it's true of bodies first. The feet matter as much as the head. Fourth, part by part. Gratitude for a body doesn't have to wait until it's well or young or the shape you'd like. A body that's tired, sore, scarred or ill has still carried you here. Thanks can be given to it exactly as it is.
screen: `FEARFULLY AND WONDERFULLY MADE.` · `A BLESSING FOR OPENINGS.` · `NO PART CAN SAY NO NEED.` · `PART BY PART.` · then, large: `THANK YOUR BODY.`

segments.voice: Sit or lie comfortably. Start at your feet: notice them, and silently say thank you. Move to your legs, and thank them for every step. Your belly, for digesting your meals. Your chest and lungs, for every breath, including this one. Your heart, for keeping time. Your hands, your arms, your shoulders, carrying so much. Your face, your eyes, your ears. If a part hurts or is hard to thank, you can simply notice it and move on. If you pray, you can turn the thanks toward God. The bell holds the time.
Asher Yatzar, the Jewish blessing thanking God who formed the body with wisdom, openings and all. Today's word.
Your line: thank you, body. Today, once when you stand up or sit down, pause and thank the part that did the work. Day eight hundred thirteen.

814.title: A small ending
814.hook: each sunset is a small ending
814.howItsDone: Muslims pray Maghrib just after sunset; Jews begin Shabbat and holy days at sundown; some Christians pray vespers or compline in the evening, and Sikhs recite Rehras Sahib at dusk.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Asher Yatzar: the psalm's fearfully and wonderfully made, and thanks part by part. Your line was thank you, body. Which part did you thank when you stood up? Today, an ending that happens every single day. Day eight hundred fourteen.

Late afternoon light goes gold, then orange, then thin. The shadows stretch across the parking lot. Somebody on a beach claps when the last edge of the sun slips under the water, and nobody can quite say why. A day is ending, the way days always do, and for a few minutes people stop to watch it end. This block of the path is about death, and the largest ending can only be imagined. A smaller one comes around every evening, and it can be watched. Today: the sunset, in a teacher's weariness, a creation refrain and a prayer time.
screen: `THE LIGHT GOES GOLD.` → `SOMEONE CLAPS AT SUNSET.` → `AN ENDING EVERY EVENING.`

segments.voice: First, the sun goes down and hastes. Ecclesiastes watches the sky and sees a loop: "The sun also ariseth, and the sun goeth down, and hasteth to his place where he arose." The writer sounds a little weary of it. But read another way, the line holds a quiet comfort. Every ending in it is also on its way to a return. Second, evening comes first. In Genesis, the days of creation close with a refrain: "And the evening and the morning were the first day." Evening is named before morning. Jewish tradition reads this as one reason the day, and so Shabbat, begins at sundown. In this way of counting, the ending of the light is where a new day starts. Third, a prayer at the setting of the sun. In Islam, Maghrib, the sunset prayer, is prayed just after the sun goes down, so the end of each day is marked by stopping and turning toward prayer. Other paths keep evening prayers too: some Christians pray vespers or compline, and Sikhs recite Rehras Sahib at dusk. The day's end gets a ritual of its own. Fourth, watch one end. A sunset is an ending you can practice on. It's safe, it's beautiful, and it always finishes. Watching one all the way through, without looking away to your phone, trains something small: letting a thing be over, and finding that the world is still there afterward.
screen: `THE SUN GOES DOWN AND HASTES.` · `EVENING COMES FIRST.` · `A PRAYER AT THE SETTING SUN.` · `WATCH ONE END.` · then, large: `A SMALL ENDING.`

segments.voice: If the sun is setting where you are, go to a window and watch it. If not, choose another small ending you can see through: the last of your breath going out, a candle you blow out, the final note of a song. Watch it to the very end. Don't hurry it and don't look away. When it's over, stay a moment in the quiet after. Notice what's still here. If you pray, an evening prayer from your own tradition can fit this moment. The bell holds the time.
Maghrib, the Muslim sunset prayer that marks the day's end, like the sun in Ecclesiastes that hastens back to where it rose. Today's word.
Your line: watch one thing end. Tonight, watch one thing end all the way through, the light, a meal, a conversation, and notice what's still there afterward. Day eight hundred fourteen.

815.title: Awake again
815.hook: Muslims wake thanking God who gave life after sleep, a small death (Bukhari)
815.howItsDone: Muslims say a short remembrance on waking, praising God who gave life after sleep, as reported of the Prophet in Sahih al-Bukhari; Jews say Modeh Ani on waking, giving thanks for the returned soul.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sun that goes down and hastes back to where it rose. Your line was watch one thing end. Did you watch one thing end all the way through? Today, the other side of that ending: the morning. Day eight hundred fifteen.

The alarm goes off. Before the phone, before the news, before the first worry of the day arrives, there's a second or two when you're simply here again. Eyes open, ceiling, light at the edge of the curtain. Usually that moment slips by unnoticed. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is reported to have filled it with a few words of thanks, and the words are still said on waking. Today: a morning line that treats every waking as a small return from something like death.
screen: `THE ALARM GOES OFF.` → `A SECOND OF SIMPLY BEING HERE.` → `A FEW WORDS ON WAKING.`

segments.voice: First, sleep as a small death. The Qur'an draws the comparison itself. In paraphrase of Surah thirty-nine, verse forty-two: God takes souls at the time of their death, and takes the souls of those who have not died during their sleep; He keeps those for whom He has decreed death, and sends the others back until an appointed time. In that picture, every night is a letting go, and every morning is a sending back. Second, the first words of the day. In Sahih al-Bukhari, a companion reports that when the Prophet ﷺ went to bed he would say, in God's name I die and I live. And when he woke he would say, in paraphrase: praise be to God, who gave us life after He had caused us to die, and to Him is the return. These words are kept as a morning remembrance, a dhikr, said on waking. Third, to Him is the return. The last phrase matters. Waking isn't treated as proof that the end has been dodged. The same breath that gives thanks for this morning remembers that there's a final return still ahead. Gratitude and honesty sit in one sentence. Fourth, a neighbor's morning line. Jews have a short morning prayer, Modeh Ani, said on waking, thanking God for returning the soul with compassion. Two traditions, each in its own words, meet the morning the same way: as something given back. For anyone, whatever they believe, the practice underneath is simple. Notice that you woke up, and let the first words be thanks.
screen: `SLEEP, A SMALL DEATH.` · `THE FIRST WORDS OF THE DAY.` · `TO HIM IS THE RETURN.` · `A NEIGHBOR'S MORNING LINE.` · then, large: `AWAKE AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes for a moment, as if the day were over and you were drifting toward sleep. Let the body grow heavy. Rest there for a few breaths, letting go of the day. Now, slowly, open your eyes, as if waking. Notice the light, the room, the fact of being here again. Let one word of thanks rise, in whatever words are yours. If you're Muslim, the Prophet's morning words may already be on your lips; if you pray in another way, your own morning prayer belongs here. Then rest, awake. The bell holds the time.
Awake again. Waking as a small return, met with thanks, as in the Prophet's morning words: praise be to God, who gave us life after He caused us to die. Today's word.
Your line: to Him is the return. Tomorrow morning, before you touch your phone, let your very first words be thanks, in whatever words are yours. Day eight hundred fifteen.

816.title: Welcoming birth
816.hook: the other end of life: traditions welcome birth
816.howItsDone: Muslim families may whisper the adhan in a newborn's right ear; Sikh families name a child from a passage of the Guru Granth Sahib; Christian families may baptize or dedicate children, and Jewish families may hold a naming or a brit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Prophet's first words on waking. Your line was to Him is the return. Were your first words this morning thanks? Today, a different kind of waking: a life arriving. Day eight hundred sixteen.

A hospital corridor at three in the morning, or a bedroom at home, or a car that didn't make it in time. A small, furious, astonished person has just arrived, and the room changes. This stretch of the path has been about the end of life: rites for the dying, words for the grieving, letters for after. It would be lopsided to leave out the other end. The traditions that mourn the dead also have ways of greeting the newborn. Today: three welcomes, from three homes, each in its own words.
screen: `A SMALL PERSON ARRIVES.` → `THE OTHER END OF LIFE.` → `THREE WELCOMES.`

segments.voice: First, a waiting man holds a baby. In Luke's Gospel, Mary and Joseph bring the infant Jesus to the Temple, and a man named Simeon, who has been told he won't see death before he sees the Lord's Christ, takes him: "Then took he him up in his arms, and blessed God." His song follows, and it begins with his own death: "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace." At the very start of one life, another man says he's ready to go. Birth and death, in one pair of arms. Second, a call whispered in the ear. In Muslim tradition, the call to prayer, the adhan, may be softly spoken into a newborn's right ear, so that among the first words the child hears are the words that call people to prayer. Some hadith collections report the Prophet ﷺ doing this for his grandson. Third, a name from an open page. In a Sikh naming ceremony, the family gathers before the Guru Granth Sahib, the scripture is opened, and a passage is read. The first letter of that passage guides the first letter of the child's name. The scripture, in a sense, joins in the naming. Fourth, welcome in other homes. Elsewhere, Christian families may baptize or dedicate a child, Jewish families may hold a naming or a brit, Hindu families have their own rites for name and first food, and Buddhist families may bring a baby for blessing. Each has its own meaning, kept in its own home. What they share is simple: a new person is not just born, but received.
screen: `SIMEON HOLDS A BABY.` · `A CALL WHISPERED IN THE EAR.` · `A NAME FROM AN OPEN PAGE.` · `WELCOME IN OTHER HOMES.` · then, large: `WELCOMING BIRTH.`

segments.voice: Think of someone new in your life, or about to be: a baby in the family or among friends, a new neighbor, a new colleague, a child just starting school. Hold them in mind for a few breaths. Let a sense of welcome gather, the way it might if you were holding them. If you pray, you can bless them in the words of your own tradition. Then decide one small act of welcome for today: a note, a meal, a greeting, a name remembered. Rest. The bell holds the time.
Welcoming birth. How traditions receive a new life: Simeon's arms, the adhan in a newborn's ear, a Sikh name from an open page. Today's word.
Your line: welcome. Today, do one small act of welcome for someone new, and say their name when you do it. Day eight hundred sixteen.

817.title: They differ
817.hook: rebirth, resurrection, return, nothing, mystery: kept apart, each in its home
817.carry: each stays in its own home
817.howItsDone: Traditions teach different things about death: Buddhists and Hindus speak of rebirth in their own distinct ways, Christians and Muslims of resurrection and judgment, Sikhs of going home, and some philosophers of nothing at all. Interfaith settings often let each speak for itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the other end of life: welcoming birth. Your line was welcome. Did someone new get a welcome from you? Today, back to the end, and to the answers, one at a time. Day eight hundred seventeen.

Five doors in one hallway, each with a different name on it. Behind one, a life comes back in a new body. Behind another, the dead are raised. Behind the third, the spirit goes back to where it came from. The fourth opens onto nothing at all. The fifth won't open, and the people who built it say that is the honest answer. For weeks now this block has walked past each door, one at a time. Today we stand in the hallway, look at all five, and don't knock down a single wall between them.
screen: `FIVE DOORS, ONE HALLWAY.` → `NO WALLS KNOCKED DOWN.`

segments.voice: First, rebirth. Buddhists teach rebirth shaped by karma, without a fixed soul passing from life to life. The Bhagavad Gita gives a Hindu picture: as a person casts off worn clothes and puts on new ones, the self casts off worn bodies. Two homes, two vocabularies, and they don't say the same thing. Second, resurrection. In John's Gospel, Jesus tells Martha, "I am the resurrection, and the life." Christians hope for the raising of the dead. The Qur'an says every soul shall taste death, and speaks of a Day of Resurrection when each soul is paid what it earned. Third, return. Ecclesiastes says, "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it." At Sikh funerals the bedtime prayer, Kirtan Sohila, is sung, and death is spoken of as going home. Fourth, nothing, or mystery. Lucretius taught that the ages after death will trouble us no more than the ages before birth. Socrates kept two options open: dreamless sleep, or a journey. Confucius, asked about death, turned the question back to life. So the block lands here: they differ. Set a Buddhist teacher's answer beside a Christian priest's, and this path doesn't read them as two versions of one answer. Each answer lives inside a whole way of life, with its own texts, rites and hopes. Pulled out and blended, each one loses what makes it make sense. So each stays in its own home, and anyone can visit.
screen: `FIRST, REBIRTH.` · `SECOND, RESURRECTION.` · `THIRD, RETURN.` · `FOURTH, NOTHING, OR MYSTERY.` · then, large: `THEY DIFFER.`

segments.voice: Take a pen, or open a note. On the first day of this block, the invitation was to write what you think now. Today, write again, a few lines only: what do you think happens at death, or what do you honestly not know? Use your own words, not a borrowed sentence, unless that sentence really is yours. If you kept what you wrote on that first day, you can set the two side by side later, without grading either one. When the lines are done, put the pen down and sit quietly with them. The bell holds the time.
They differ. Rebirth, resurrection, return, nothing, mystery: real answers from real traditions, each kept in its own home, never blended into one. Today's word.
Your line: each stays in its own home. Today, if death comes up in conversation, ask someone what their tradition says, and listen without fitting it into yours. Day eight hundred seventeen.

818.title: Death close
818.hook: sixty days facing the end, to live better now
818.howItsDone: People on many paths keep death in view as a way of living more fully: Psalm 90 is read in Jewish and Christian worship, Stoics wrote notes to themselves about the end, and some readers return to Thoreau's Walden for its call to live deliberately.

segments.voice: Yesterday, five doors in one hallway. Your line was each stays in its own home. Did anyone tell you what their door says? Today, the last day of facing the end, and the first step back outside. Day eight hundred eighteen.

This block has run sixty days. It opened with the oldest question, and a page where you wrote what you think. Since then: Socrates weighing sleep against a journey, the Buddha's last words, a boy waiting at Death's door, a mourner's prayer that never mentions death, Martha and the resurrection, an atom's weight of good, Zhuangzi's skull, marigolds and lanterns, hospice nurses, tea, an ethical will. Today the block closes, and it closes on the point the whole thing was for.
screen: `SIXTY DAYS.` →`THE OLDEST QUESTION.` → `WHAT IT WAS FOR.`

segments.voice: First, number our days, the psalm this block already sat with once. It asks, "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." The counting isn't there to frighten. It's there to make a heart wise, now. Second, the woods. Thoreau went to live by Walden Pond, and he said why: "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived." Death is in the sentence, but the sentence is about living. Third, back to the day. Marcus, in his notebook, wrote of passing each day as if it were the last, neither frantic nor numb, so the day in front of him would be done well. Different homes, one direction of travel: the end looked at squarely, and then the face turned back toward today. Fourth, live, then. That is the line this block ends on. It isn't a promise about what happens after. The traditions differ on that, and we left them differing. It's what these teachers did once they had looked at death: they went back into the day, a little more awake.
screen: `NUMBER OUR DAYS.` · `THE WOODS.` · `BACK TO THE DAY.` · `LIVE, THEN.` · then, large: `DEATH CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Go outside, if you can. A step, a balcony or an open window is enough. Stand or sit where the air moves. Breathe in, and notice that it's this air, today's air. Breathe out, and let the sixty days be finished. There's nothing to conclude. If you like, say the line silently on each out-breath: live, then. Let your eyes find one thing out there that is alive, a tree, a bird, a person walking past, and stay with it. The bell holds the time.
Walden Pond. Where Thoreau went to live deliberately and front only the essential facts of life. Today's word.
Your line: live, then. Today, do one ordinary thing deliberately, as Thoreau put it: a meal, a walk, a conversation, done awake. Tomorrow a new block begins, on love. Day eight hundred eighteen.

819.title: Many words for love
819.hook: Greek philia and agape, Hebrew chesed, Arabic mahabba, Sanskrit bhakti: each with its own flavor
819.howItsDone: Each tradition has its own vocabulary of love: Christians speak of agape, Jews of chesed, Sufi Muslims of mahabba, Hindus of bhakti, and the Greek philosophers of philia. Each is taught and practiced in its own setting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Walden Pond: sixty days ended. Your line was live, then. Did you do one ordinary thing awake? This week thanked a body, watched a sunset end, woke up thankful, welcomed a birth, kept the answers apart and stepped outside. Today, a new question: love. Day eight hundred nineteen.

English makes one word work very hard. The same love goes to a spouse, a grandmother, a best friend, a dog, a city, a song and a sandwich. Nobody is confused, exactly, but a lot gets packed into four letters. Other languages, and the traditions that speak them, keep several words on the shelf, each with its own flavor. So the love block opens there: not with a definition, but with a handful of words, each from its own home, each naming something the others don't.
screen: `ONE WORD, WORKING HARD.` → `SEVERAL WORDS ON THE SHELF.`

segments.voice: First, two Greek words. Philia is the love of friends, the warmth of people who choose each other. Aristotle writes about it at length, and we'll meet him in a few days. Agape is a word the New Testament uses for the love of God and of neighbor. The first letter of John says, "God is love," and the Greek word there is agape. Second, a Hebrew word. Chesed is loyal, steady kindness, love that keeps its promises. The King James Bible renders it more than one way, often as mercy or lovingkindness. Psalm 136 repeats it again and again: "for his mercy endureth for ever." Third, an Arabic word. Mahabba is love, and Sufi writers in Islam used it for the love between God and the seeker. The Qur'an speaks of a people whom God loves and who love Him. Fourth, a Sanskrit word. Bhakti is devotion, love turned toward God. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that whoever offers him even a leaf, a flower, a fruit or a little water with devotion, he accepts it. Each word has a home, and a flavor you lose if you swap it for another. They aren't five labels for one thing. They're different loves, named by people who noticed something particular about each.
screen: `TWO GREEK WORDS.` · `CHESED, LOYAL KINDNESS.` · `MAHABBA, IN SUFI WRITING.` · `BHAKTI, DEVOTION.` · then, large: `MANY WORDS FOR LOVE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Now bring to mind the loves in your life, one at a time, and see which word fits each. A friend you chose: maybe philia. Someone you've stayed loyal to through hard years: maybe chesed. A love that reaches toward something larger, if you have one: maybe bhakti or mahabba. A plain wish for a stranger's good: maybe agape. There's no right answer, and no need to find every kind. Just notice how many loves are already there. The bell holds the time.
Chesed. A Hebrew word for loyal, steady kindness, one of four loves this lesson named, each with its own flavor. Today's word.
Your line: many words. Today, each time you say love, pause half a second and ask which kind you mean. Day eight hundred nineteen.

fork.setup: in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna speaks of what a devoted person can offer. what does he say he accepts?
options: only great sacrifices.
even a leaf, a flower, a fruit or a little water, offered with devotion.
nothing; devotion needs no offering.
fork.reveal: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water. in bhakti, the devotion is what counts, not the size of the gift.

original.note: Hebrew: loyal, steady kindness; the King James Bible often renders it mercy or lovingkindness.

trapdoor: what you thought: love is love; the word doesn't matter.
what it means: traditions named different loves: friendship, loyal kindness, devotion, the love of God and neighbor.
what a scholar hears: one English word stands in for several, so when a translation says love, it's worth asking which word sits underneath.
